The Effects of Sleep on Memory Consolidation in Undergraduates

Maria Lopez

Department of Psychology, State University

PSY 301: Research Methods

Dr. Kim

May 2, 2026

Abstract

This study examined whether sleep duration predicts recall in a sample of undergraduates. Participants who slept more than seven hours recalled more words; however, the effect was small.

The Effects of Sleep on Memory Consolidation in Undergraduates

Sleep seems to play a role in memory, although the mechanism remains debated (Walker, 2017; Stickgold & Walker, 2013). Earlier work suggests that slow-wave sleep supports the transfer of information from the hippocampus to the cortex (Diekelmann & Born, 2010, p. 115).

Method

Participants

Forty-two undergraduates took part in exchange for course credit. Most were first-year students; a few were older transfer students.

Results

Participants who slept longer recalled more words, r = .31, p = .04. This result is likely to be fragile, given the sample size.

Discussion

To some extent, these findings support the consolidation account. I think future studies should measure sleep with actigraphy rather than self-report.

References

Diekelmann, S., & Born, J. (2010). The memory function of sleep. Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 11(2), 114-126. https://doi.org/10.1038/nrn2762

Stickgold, R., & Walker, M. P. (2013). Sleep-dependent memory triage. Nature Neuroscience, 16(2), 139-145.

Walker, M. (2017). Why we sleep: Unlocking the power of sleep and dreams. Scribner.
